title: Research environment built and host toolchain verified
detail: libimobiledevice 1.2.1 win-x64 extracted; idevice_id -l exits 0, confirming usbmux transport works. Apple Mobile Device Service 19.4 installed and running. a9id.py enumerates Apple USB devices and classifies mode from PID.

title: libirecovery is Windows-native; WSL is NOT required for DFU work
detail: irecovery.exe -h confirms full DFU capability (query, mode, payload, command, shell, file, normal-reboot) from the already-extracted libimobiledevice win-x64 bundle. An earlier plan draft assumed Linux/macOS was required for bootrom tooling; that assumption was unverified and is now disproven. ipwndfu remains Linux-first and will need WinUSB bound to the DFU device node.

title: WSL Ubuntu-24.04 unusable; podman-main unaffected
detail: wsl --shutdown does not repair Ubuntu-24.04: 'Failed to start the systemd user session for root' then 'execvpe(/bin/echo) failed: I/O error'. podman-main reports Running. Non-blocking because irecovery is Windows-native.

title: Target device hardware confirmed intact: screen and buttons reliable
detail: iPhone SE 1st gen is physically near-new with an undamaged screen. This clears the DFU-entry obstacle: checkm8 requires precise button timing with no visual feedback (Power+VolDown ~8s, release Power, hold VolDown ~10s), which is unreliable on damaged hardware. It also means hardware faults will not confound measurements - unlike the Samsung, where host/port/cable hypotheses had to be eliminated experimentally over several hours. A clean device provides a trustworthy baseline.

title: Four PLAN.md errors corrected: KTRR is A10+, A9 uses KPP/WatchTower
detail: Primary-source review (Siguza KTRR, xerub Tick-Tock, ipwndfu/checkm8.py, libirecovery) disproved four claims in the original plan. (1) KTRR does NOT exist on A9 - Siguza states it is A10 and later, relying on A10-only AMCC RoRgn + KTRR_*_EL1 registers. A9 uses KPP/WatchTower: a SOFTWARE monitor iBoot loads at 0x4100000000 in TrustZone EL3, bypassed publicly in yalu102. Layer 3 is MORE reachable than assumed, not less. (2) checkm8 is CVE-2019-8900 (CERT VU#941987), not CVE-2019-8566 family. (3) Linux-on-A9 was wrongly called impossible: mainline carries A9 DTs for s8000/s8003 in arch/arm64/boot/dts/apple, but they are BRING-UP ONLY (memory/chosen 'to be filled by loader', spin-table CPUs, UART+AIC+pinctrl+watchdog only, framebuffer disabled). Correct wording: upstream and bootable-in-principle via a checkm8-based loader, but no publicly demonstrated general-purpose foreign OS. (4) a9id.py labelled A9 as s5l8960x, which is actually A7 (iPhone 5s); A9 is s8000/s8003. A9-PPL remains UNVERIFIED - do not design around it.
repro: python P:\Reverseing\Arlo\a9lab\a9id.py; see PLAN.md layer-3 correction block
source: subagent RQ1 brief, primary sources cited therein

title: ipwndfu CANNOT exploit A9; gaster HAS a dedicated A9 payload
detail: Upstream ipwndfu checkm8.py all_exploit_configs() covers s5l8947x/8950x/8955x/8960x, t8002, t8004, t8010, t8011, t8015 - s8000/s8003 appear only under a never-implemented 'future SoC support' comment, so ipwndfu -p exits 'not a compatible device'. It is also Python 2, hard-requires the libusb1 backend, and its README says it will not work in a VM. RESOLUTION: verified by fetching the repo listing that gaster (0x7FF/gaster) ships payload_A9.S and payload_A9.bin alongside payload_notA9.S - an explicit, dedicated A9 payload path. A search also surfaced LukeZGD/gaster, a fork described as 'Checkm8 experiment to understand AP/SEP internals', which aligns with RQ3. NOTE: A9 takes a SIMPLER exploit path than A10/A11 - per the writeup, A8/A8X/A9 need no memory-leak or heap-feng-shui stage and achieve direct code execution without ROP/JOP. Do NOT port A10/A11 payloads to A9.
repro: github.com/0x7FF/gaster file listing; ipwndfu checkm8.py all_exploit_configs()
source: subagent RQ1 brief + direct repo inspection

title: SRTG is the SecureROM-vs-iBSS gate; PID 0x1227 is shared by both
detail: A9 SecureROM DFU and iBSS/LLB DFU both present USB PID 0x1227, so the PID alone cannot tell them apart. checkm8 matches SRTG in the USB serial string and refuses to run against iBSS DFU with 'CPID is compatible, but serial number string does not match'. Therefore SRTG MUST be read and confirmed before any exploit attempt. All of CPID/CPRV/CPFM/SCEP/BDID/ECID/IBFL/SRNM/IMEI/SRTG are parsed PRE-AUTHENTICATION by plain substring scans of the USB serial string descriptor (irecv_load_device_info_from_iboot_string) with no signature check - so this is free, read-only reconnaissance available the moment the device enumerates in DFU.
repro: irecovery.exe -q with device in DFU; libirecovery irecv_load_device_info_from_iboot_string()

title: iPhone SE battery reported in perfect state; swelling risk cleared
detail: Owner reports the battery is in perfect condition and the device is physically clean with no drops. This clears the swollen-cell risk that a multi-year deep discharge would otherwise imply, and removes the 'worn cell' concern that two years of use would suggest. DFU entry and charging can proceed without the lay-flat/wobble check. Note this is user-reported condition, not a measured cycle count or battery-health percentage - that can be read via ideviceinfo BatteryCurrentCapacity once the device boots, and the definitive figure is Settings > Battery > Battery Health on-device.
repro: n/a - owner-reported; verify via ideviceinfo once booted

title: SILENT TRAP: bind libusbK not WinUSB for DFU, or checkm8 fails with no error
detail: checkm8 calls device.reset() twice. libusb 1.0.24 source states Windows/WinUSB cannot perform a host-initiated reset - 'the best we can do is cycle the pipes (and even then, the control pipe can not be reset using WinUSB)' (windows_winusb.c:3083-3091). Only libusbK/libusb0 actually call ResetDevice (:3124-3128). If WinUSB is bound, the reset stages are SILENT NO-OPS: the exploit fails with 'Exploit failed. Device did not enter pwned DFU Mode' and NO underlying error, so one would debug the wrong layer for hours. ACTION: bind libusbK via Zadig to the DFU node VID 0x05AC PID 0x1227. Note the irony: for the Samsung we had to REMOVE WinUSB so usbser.sys could bind; here we must ADD a libusb driver and specifically NOT WinUSB.

title: irecovery -k is limera1n-ONLY; verified via DLL exports (my earlier inference was wrong)
detail: I previously inferred from the '-k, --payload send limera1n usb exploit payload' help text that irecovery could deliver a checkm8 payload on Windows. That inference was WRONG. Verified two independent ways this session: (1) symbol inspection of the local irecovery.dll shows irecv_trigger_limera1n_exploit EXPORTED and irecv_trigger_checkm8_exploit ABSENT entirely; (2) upstream tools/irecovery.c routes -k to irecv_trigger_limera1n_exploit(), implemented limera1n-only in src/libirecovery.c, which on non-Apple platforms degenerates to a single synchronous 0x21/2 transfer with none of the macOS abort-thread trick. limera1n targets S5L8920/8922 (A4-era); A9 needs checkm8. irecovery is therefore useful ONLY AFTER pwn (-q, -c, -f, -s) and is NOT the exploit path.
repro: irecovery.dll GetProcAddress for irecv_trigger_checkm8_exploit returns absent

title: Windows exploit path: gaster has payload_A9; King (pgarba) claims Windows+libusbK
detail: Upstream ipwndfu is a dead end on Windows for two reasons: (a) it cannot exploit A9 at all - its SoC table lists s8000/s8003 only under a never-implemented future-support comment; (b) it is Python 2 exclusively (print statements, basestring, decode('hex'), tostring, cStringIO, raw_input) so Python 3.14 dies at PARSE TIME before any USB call. It also hard-requires the libusb1 backend and its README says it will not work in a VM. VIABLE ALTERNATIVES: gaster (0x7FF/gaster) ships payload_A9.S and payload_A9.bin plus #ifdef WIN32 - verified by direct repo listing. King (pgarba/King, 'port of checkm8 to C', 140 stars, pushed 2024-06) explicitly claims Windows support with libusbK via Zadig and lists iPhone SE in supported devices - SECONDHAND, not built or run. Note ipwndfu has NO Linux-only code in the exploit path (no /dev, udev, getuid, setuid, dfu-util); it is a pure EP0 control-transfer client via vendored pyusb.
repro: github.com/0x7FF/gaster file listing (payload_A9.bin); github.com/pgarba/King API metadata

title: King BUILT for Windows: king.exe produced from source, A9 path confirmed in code
detail: King (pgarba/King checkm8 C port) compiled successfully on this Windows host with MSVC 19.44 + nmake + CMake 4.3.4, linking libusb 1.0.30 x64 MSVC DLL flavour. Output king.exe 123 KB, NMAKE_EXIT=0. Two build fixes were required and are now scripted: (1) King's dfu.h does #include <libusb-1.0/libusb.h>, so the header must ALSO exist at include/libusb-1.0/libusb.h - without it the build dies with C1083; (2) libusb-1.0.dll must sit beside king.exe since it links dynamically. king.exe runs and reports usage: checkm8, enable_jtag, read32, read64, decryptIMG, hexdump, dump-rom. VERIFIED IN SOURCE: runCheckm8() dispatches on the DFU serial string and routes CPID:7000 CPRV:11 (A8), CPID:8000 CPRV:20 (A9) and CPID:8003 CPRV:01 (A9) to a dedicated checkm8_A8_A9() function - i.e. our device takes its own code path, not the generic one. constants_checkm8_s8000 exists. Reproducible build script written to a9lab/build-king.ps1. STILL UNVERIFIED: never run against a real device; libusbK is not yet bound (libusbK - NOT WinUSB - is mandatory because WinUSB cannot perform the host-initiated device.reset() that checkm8 requires, and failure is silent).
source: own build + source inspection of main.cpp

title: A9 DFU CPID is 8000/8003 - confirmed by King dispatch; 8010 is T8010/A10
detail: Resolved a self-inflicted doubt: King's README example shows CPID:8010, which briefly made me question the recorded A9 CPID values. Reading main.cpp runCheckm8() resolves it definitively - the A8/A9 branch matches CPID:7000 CPRV:11, CPID:8000 CPRV:20 and CPID:8003 CPRV:01. CPID 0x8010 belongs to a DIFFERENT SoC: T8010 = A10 = iPhone 7, which takes the generic checkm8() path with t8010_overwrite and iBoot-2696.0.0.1.33, NOT the A8/A9 path. So A9 in DFU reports CPID 8000 or 8003 (the same model can present either depending on fab: s8000 Maui/Samsung vs s8003 Malta/TSMC), and the a9id.py reference table was correct as written. Lesson recorded: do not 'fix' notes on the strength of a README example - read the dispatch code.
